title: Michael Heidelberger developed a pneumonia vaccine that was successfully tested on Air Force recruits in 1944

trailer.text: Before sulfonamides and penicillin, pneumonia filled city hospitals every winter.
During World War II Heidelberger developed a simple vaccine against pneumococcal pneumonia, a serious health threat to soldiers.
According to the National Library of Medicine, the vaccine was successfully tested in 1944 among Army Air Force recruits.

According to the obituary published in 2001, at that time it was generally recommended that people at high risk of pneumococcal pneumonia, especially the elderly, receive each autumn an injection of a mixture of pneumococcal polysaccharides.

stations.title: A Jewish family in New York

paragraphs.text: Heidelberger was born in 1888 in New York.
His grandfather was a German Jew who emigrated to the United States.
According to the National Library of Medicine, he had a younger brother born 21 months after him.
Every winter, outbreaks of pneumonia overloaded city hospitals.
Pneumonia is the principal disease caused by the pneumococcus bacterium.
In some outbreaks, up to a quarter of patients with type II pneumococcus died.
Through most of the 1920s and 1930s there was only one effective treatment.
The patient received an injection of serum matched to the type of his bacterium, and pharmaceutical companies produced it from horses and rabbits.
To treat, the exact type of bacterium had to be identified in each patient.
Those alive at the time remember how families dreaded hearing that a family member had pneumonia.
In 1917, after the United States declared war on Germany, Heidelberger was appointed an officer in the Medical Corps and assigned to the Rockefeller Institute.
There he developed with Jacobs a drug against African sleeping sickness, for which he received the Belgian Order of Leopold II.
The researcher Avery wanted Heidelberger to study what the material in the pneumococcus capsule was made of.
Flexner persuaded him to join the group studying the bacterium.
They chose type II, and the choice proved fortunate, because this bacterium was abundant and the structure of its capsule simple.
The more the capsular material was purified, the lower its nitrogen content became, which surprised the researchers.
In 1923 Heidelberger and Avery reported that this material is made of polysaccharides.
This is the material that determines the type of the bacterium.
The discovery disproved what most scientists then believed, that only proteins could act as antigens.
The Rockefeller Institute did not offer him a permanent position, and Flexner urged him to move on.
Flexner said, perhaps correctly, that Heidelberger had worked alongside researchers more senior than him, and so his achievements would be credited to them.
In 1927 Heidelberger moved to head the chemical laboratory at Mount Sinai Hospital.
A year later he moved to the College of Physicians and Surgeons at Columbia University.
Heidelberger knew a great deal about polysaccharides, and with this knowledge he developed methods for isolating pure antibodies.
In this way he proved that antibodies are proteins.
According to Encyclopedia.com, he and his colleagues at Columbia were the first to provide solid evidence of this.
His laboratory supplied antibodies to treat patients hospitalized with pneumonia.
The number of deaths from pneumonia of types I, II and III fell, which showed that treatment with purified antibodies worked.

stations.title: War, crowded camps and volunteer students

paragraphs.text: During World War II recruits lived in crowded conditions in Army camps, and studies were carried out to reduce the cases of pneumonia there.
Heidelberger then developed a simple vaccine against the disease.
In the first stage, medical students at the College of Physicians and Surgeons who volunteered received an injection of about 50 micrograms of purified polysaccharide.
Measurable amounts of antipolysaccharide antibodies were found in their blood.
The students could not be deliberately exposed to virulent bacteria, so Colin MacLeod organized a large-scale clinical trial.
MacLeod was a microbiologist and co-discoverer of the genetic properties of DNA, and the committee he headed organized the trial in 1944.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Heidelberger recommended to the Army that men at a training camp for aviators in South Dakota be vaccinated, based on the trial in students.
During the same war Heidelberger also worked on protection against anthrax and ricin, which the Germans were thought to be preparing to use against Allied forces.
Another project sought to develop, from lysed red blood cells, a vaccine to treat malaria in soldiers returning from the South Pacific.
The trial took place at an Army camp in South Dakota.
According to archival records, this was the air base in Sioux Falls.
One group received an injection of polysaccharides of types I, II, V and VII.
A control group of similar size received an injection of saline.
Sources differ on how many people took part.
Hodges oversaw the trial at the camp.
He and other medical officers on the base took part in the trial themselves.
Hodges sent Heidelberger blood samples from immunized soldiers, to check how many antibodies they contained.
The vaccinated group had far fewer cases of pneumonia of the types the vaccine covered.
The sources give different figures.
Cases of pneumonia from other types of pneumococcus occurred in about the same numbers in both groups.
According to archival records, the trial proved that a vaccine made from a mixture of polysaccharides from four types of pneumococcus is effective.
The results of the wartime trial were clear and striking, and so the vaccine continued to be used.
According to the obituary, an almost protein-free polysaccharide protected so well, and this shows how potent the antibodies it elicited were.
According to the obituary, the trial may have succeeded because the polysaccharides selectively stimulated memory B cells.

According to the obituary published in 2001, at that time it was generally recommended that people at high risk of pneumococcal pneumonia, especially the elderly, receive each autumn an injection of a mixture of pneumococcal polysaccharides.
According to the obituary published in 2001, at that time pneumococcal polysaccharides were linked in vaccines to carrier proteins.
According to the obituary, the vaccine, in modified form, is still useful almost 60 years after it was first proven in U.S. Army troops.
According to the obituary, Heidelberger's work led directly to a simple vaccine that continues to reduce illness and death from a disease that was among the most feared.
Encyclopedia.com notes that Heidelberger is generally considered the father of immunochemistry.
He received 15 honorary degrees and 46 medals, citations and awards.
Among them were two Lasker Awards, and sources differ on the year of the first.
The 1978 Lasker Award was given for studies that laid the groundwork for capsular purified polysaccharide vaccines against pneumonia and meningitis.
According to Encyclopedia.com, in 1967 he received the National Medal of Science.
After Columbia he moved to Rutgers, and from there to New York University.
Sources differ on the years of these moves.
As president of the American Association of Immunologists, he urged scientists in his addresses to resist nuclear armament and restrictions on exchanges of information between scientists.
According to the National Library of Medicine, he had a son from his first marriage who died in 1983.
Sources differ on the son's name.
He lived to the age of 103 and worked in the laboratory until a few weeks before his death.
A week before his death he was still writing a paper.
He died in New York on June 25, 1991.
According to the National Academy of Sciences obituary, Heidelberger's only son was Charles Heidelberger, a noted professor of biochemistry at the University of Wisconsin.

claims.quote: The clear and striking results of that wartime trial led to the continued use of the vaccine

claims.text: לפי ההספד, העובדה שפוליסכריד כמעט נטול חלבון הצליח להגן כל כך מעידה על עוצמת הנוגדנים שעורר.
claims.quote: That essentially protein-free pneumococcal polysaccharide injected alone was so effective in protecting against pneumococcal infection in the World War II trial testifies to the remarkable potency of the antibodies they elicited.

claims.text: לפי ההספד, ייתכן שהצלחת הניסוי נבעה מכך שהפוליסכרידים עוררו באופן סלקטיבי תאי B של זיכרון.
claims.quote: it is possible that the great success of the wartime trial organized by MacLeod came about because the protein-free polysaccharides selectively stimulated memory B cells

claims.text: כיום מקשרים פוליסכרידים של פנאומוקוק לחלבוני נשא בחיסונים.
claims.quote: Currently, therefore, pneumococcal and other bacterial polysaccharide antigens are linked in vaccines to carrier proteins

claims.text: לפי ההספד, פיתוח חיסון פשוט שבצורה מותאמת עדיין שימושי כמעט 60 שנה אחרי שיעילותו הוכחה לראשונה בחיילי צבא ארה"ב במלחמת העולם השנייה.
claims.quote: to develop a simple vaccine that in modified form is still useful almost 60 years after its effectiveness was first demonstrated in U.S. Army troops during World War II.

claims.text: לפי ההספד, עבודתו של היידלברגר הובילה ישירות לפיתוח חיסון פשוט שממשיך לצמצם תחלואה ותמותה ממחלה שהייתה מהמפחידות ביותר.
claims.quote: And his work led directly to the development of a simple vaccine that continues to this day to help reduce morbidity and mortality

claims.text: אנציקלופדיה.קום מציינת שהיידלברגר נחשב בדרך כלל לאבי האימונוכימיה.
claims.quote: chemist who is generally considered to be the father of immunochemistry.

claims.text: פרס לסקר ב-1978 ניתן על מחקרים שהניחו את היסוד לחיסונים מפוליסכריד קפסולרי מטוהר למניעת דלקת ריאות ודלקת קרום המוח.
claims.quote: which laid the groundwork for the development of capsular purified polysaccharide vaccines for the prevention of pneumonia and meningitis

claims.text: לפי הספריה הלאומית לרפואה, עם פרישתו מקולומביה ב-1954 עבר היידלברגר למכון למיקרוביולוגיה ברטגרס, וב-1963 לאוניברסיטת ניו יורק.
claims.quote: Upon his retirement from Columbia in 1954, Heidelberger moved to the Institute of Microbiology at Rutgers University, and in 1963 to the New York University School of Medicine.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, ב-1955 קיבל היידלברגר הזמנה מסלמן וקסמן להיות פרופסור אורח באימונוכימיה ברטגרס.
claims.quote: In 1955, a year before he was to reach the mandatory retirement age at Columbia, Heidelberger accepted an invitation from Selman Waksman

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, ב-1964 עזב היידלברגר את רטגרס והפך לפרופסור חבר לפתולוגיה בבית הספר לרפואה של אוניברסיטת ניו יורק.
claims.quote: Heidelberger left Rutgers in 1964 to become an adjunct professor of pathology at the New York University School of Medicine.

claims.text: בנאומיו כנשיא האגודה האמריקנית לאימונולוגים קרא היידלברגר למדענים להתנגד לחימוש גרעיני ולהגבלות על חילופי מידע בין מדענים.
claims.quote: Both times his presidential addresses urged scientists to resist nuclear armament and restrictions on free exchanges among scientists across national boundaries

claims.text: לפי הספריה הלאומית לרפואה, בנו של היידלברגר מנישואיו הראשונים היה צ'ארלס, ביולוג סרטן בולט שמת ב-1983.
claims.quote: his son from his first marriage, Charles, a prominent cancer biologist who died in 1983 at the age of 63

claims.text: לפי לוח הזמנים של הספריה הלאומית לרפואה, בנו של היידלברגר מנישואיו לנינה טאכאו היה דיוויד (1920-1983).
claims.quote: Married Nina Tachau (d. 1946), with whom he had a son, David (1920-1983)

claims.text: היידלברגר חי עד גיל 103 ועבד במעבדה עד שבועות ספורים לפני מותו ב-1991.
claims.quote: he lived to be 103, and was in the laboratory until a few weeks before his death in 1991

claims.text: היידלברגר המשיך לכתוב מאמר שבוע לפני מותו בגיל 103.
claims.quote: was writing a paper a week before his death at the age of 103

claims.text: היידלברגר נפטר בניו יורק ב-25 ביוני 1991.
claims.quote: 1991 --Died in New York City, June 25th

claims.text: לפי ההספד של האקדמיה הלאומית למדעים, בנו היחיד של היידלברגר היה צ'ארלס היידלברגר, פרופסור נודע לביוכימיה באוניברסיטת ויסקונסין.
claims.quote: his only child, Charles Heidelberger

claims.text: היידלברגר נולד ב-1888 בניו יורק.
claims.quote: Michael Heidelberger was born in New York City in 1888.

claims.text: צ'ארלס
claims.quote: Michael and his younger brother, Charles J. Heidelberger.
